extracted.intended_audience: readers, students, and critics of literary/philosophical fiction (esp. Carlyle's Sartor Resartus); editors of literary texts
extracted.subtask_description: Interpreting and editing a 19th-century philosophical-satirical prose work (Carlyle's Sartor Resartus): how to read its metaphors, biographical claims, and editorial presentation. Emphasizes hermeneutic principles and editorial responsibilities for such material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of Wonder / Mysticism over reductive Science
rubrics_metrics.description: The habit of wonder (mysticism) is the proper temper; scientific Mensuration/Numeration that destroys wonder is suspect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teufelsdrockh insists 'Wonder is the basis of Worship' and condemns a Science that would turn the mind into an 'Arithmetical Mill' (memory as hopper, tables as meal). 'Thought without Reverence is barren, perhaps poisonous'; the skeptic who cannot wonder is 'but a Pair of Spectacles behind which there is no Eye.' Avoid purely logical/explanatory accounts that elide mystery; value reverence and the sustaining power of wonder in interpretation and writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy of Clothes: treat visible things as emblems
rubrics_metrics.description: All visible things (clothes, objects, language) are garments or emblems that body forth spirit or ideas and therefore must be read symbolically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly asserts 'All visible things are emblems' and 'Matter...is Spirit, the manifestation of Spirit.' Examples: King's mantle and ox-goad both have prose/poetry and reverend worth; language is 'the Flesh-Garment' of thought. In criticism or composition, read mundane details as windows into larger metaphysical meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: See through outward 'clothes' to the person beneath
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic/reader should look past social/official garments to apprehend the inward person or spiritual reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted advice: 'Happy he who can look through the Clothes of a Man...into the Man himself' — even a Dread Potentate may be an 'incompetent Digestive-apparatus' yet also an 'inscrutable venerable Mystery.' Practice sympathetic, penetrating reading that recognizes dignity in the meanest figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language is the bodily expression of thought; metaphors are essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Language is the 'body' of thought; metaphors are its muscles and tissues — creative, constitutive elements of meaning rather than mere ornament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage: 'Language is called the Garment of Thought: however, it should rather be, Language is the Flesh-Garment, the Body, of Thought.' 'Metaphors are her stuff' — thus writers and critics should accept metaphor as fundamental and expect no 'unmetaphorical style.' Evaluate styles by their muscularity (vigor), pallor (deadness), or flush (vitality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate genuine metaphors from sham/ornamental ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all metaphors are good; some are deceptive, superfluous, or tawdry and should be rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author warns of 'sham Metaphors' that 'overhanging that same Thought's-Body...may be called its false stuffings, superfluous show-cloaks (_Putz-Mantel_), and tawdry woollen rags.' The critic/writer should identify and remove such false ornamentation — 'whereof he that runs and reads may gather whole hampers,--and burn them.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Names as formative: the significance of naming
rubrics_metrics.description: Names are an early and powerful garment for the self; naming shapes identity, behavior, and literary meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle argues 'there is much, nay almost all, in Names' and that naming is the earliest clothing of the 'ME.' Examples: Adam's naming task, the conjectural power in the name 'Diogenes Teufelsdrockh.' Critics should attend to names as intentional signals and formative devices in interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biography/autobiography required to understand a life-philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: A life-philosophy (Lebensphilosophie) that originates in character must be grounded in the biographical context of its author to be fully comprehended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Hofrath (Heuschrecke) insists that the Character and 'Author's View of the World' be known: 'till the Author's View of the World...are clear: in short till a Biography of him has been philosophico-poetically written.' Editorial apparatus and biographical materials are necessary to interpret a work that claims to be a life-philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial duty: selection, order, and method to impose coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: An editor must collate miscellaneous, chaotic materials with method (union of like with like) to produce a coherent presentation; selection and ordering are substantive interpretive acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Editor describes the Six Paper-Bags' chaotic contents and his task to build a 'firm Bridge for British travellers' from the weltering deep. His labor (collating, deciphering, arranging) is heroic and affects meaning; criticism should acknowledge editorial shaping and the necessity of method to turn chaos into intelligible work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interconnectedness/holism of Nature and meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing is truly detached; every object and event participates in a universal system of forces and meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: the smithy-fire 'kindled at the Sun', 'fed by air that circulates from before Noah's Deluge', 'a little ganglion...in the great vital system of Immensity.' Critics and writers should favor holistic readings that trace affinities and forces across apparently disparate phenomena.
